chunks.text: Nice.

Well, hello. Hi, Ian, and welcome back to the select committee. I know that this briefing has been a long time coming, with a few bits and pieces happening, and this committee being quite busy with RMA reform. But welcome to the committee this afternoon. We look forward to your presentation.

And look, really, we are in your hands. We have got the documents and if you want to talk us through your presentation. Thank you very much. Chris will start us off, and yeah, we'll take it from there. Thank you so much, Catherine, for finding us the time, and a whole lot of thank yous around the room for the support for this piece of work.

So kia ora. My name's Chris Ingle. I'm with the Bay of Plenty Regional Council as a day job, as one of the general managers. But for this role, I'm the chair of the reference group that supports Ian both for his academic work and his research for the future of biodiversity in New Zealand. And with me is Brent Mountford. I'll let these guys introduce themselves.

Yeah. Yes, I'm on the reference group as well, and sheep and beef farmer up in the Bay. And as most of you most probably know, quite a conservationist, right into that sort of thing. Which bay was that? The real bay. The real bay, that's right. Well, actually, I think we lost last one. Oh, Hawke's safe.

Looking to get that back. Yeah, and also president for Federated Farmers Bay of Plenty. Ian Herbert. I am the New Zealand Biophin assessment lead. This assessment is being done independently through the Otago University Business School, where I'm completing my Doctor of Business Administration. If you're to take all of the Master of Business Administration people, all the MBAs, and find the quirky ones, they're the ones who go on and do a doctorate.

So this work is done as part of that doctorate. So thank you all very much for your time. I just want to also just acknowledge Peter, who's in the back, from the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment. Over the last two and a half years of this assessment, we've been able to reach out to them, just to let them know what we're doing, and they've been able to give us a bit of feedback, and so want to acknowledge them. Also want to acknowledge a few members of Parliament who in the past have helped with this and understand

the numbers. First of all, of course, is the Prime Minister, who does know the numbers behind the fund that we're talking about. Also would like to acknowledge Chris Hipkins, who has said, "Yep, keen to keep this on our radar." Shane Jones has asked Andy Foster to keep it on his radar.

Want to also acknowledge Simon Court, who understood the importance of having a natural capital policy to go with this. Plus Lan Pham, who is not here, who has a good understanding of this. So I just wanted to acknowledge those people before we start. So, in terms of the purpose, we'll just go to the next slide.

It is very straightforward. It is to measure New Zealand's biodiversity investment, calculate the gap between what it takes to maintain and restore our biodiversity across the country, and then reduce the deferrals. A deferral is a financial input into that purpose, and it's deferred to the next year.
So we're looking at reducing deferrals on natural capital. So that's what a Biofin purpose is. It uses biodiversity finance to break the historic cycle of biodiversity loss. So it's non-regulatory.

And if we go to the next slide. And just, members, we've only got 14 slides, so what we were hoping to do was to fly through them fairly quickly, and then have some pretty free-ranging questions and answers. And Ian's here to answer all the questions, although Brent might have some answers too. But some of these slides you may have seen if you were here at the last time we presented about a year ago. And this picture here shows how many countries in the world, 133 nations in the world, are following this identical process, the Biofin process. So this isn't something that Ian's

dreamed up in the University of Otago, although I'm sure he could if we set him to that task. But this is actually a tried and true process that's been adopted, perhaps mostly in the countries like Africa, South America, but now it's also being adopted in European countries as well.

So I think New Zealand's well-placed now to be doing this work. There's a toolbox of, I think, 150 different finance solutions, and you can select which one suits your nation. And once you've gone through this process, then it becomes obvious which ones are going to work, and that's Ian's job in this research.

So the next slide shows the process that Brent and I and the other four members of the reference group are trying to follow. Well, we are following it. And it's basically that the diagram there with the three in the middle, the arrow, if you like. With these three reports that have to be done to satisfy these requirements, and the first is already completed, the policy and institutional review.

If you haven't read it, it's really just reflecting the laws of this country and how we deliver biodiversity currently. And of course, that's changing, as you guys are well aware. The second one, which we're reporting back on today, is the biodiversity expenditure review, and that's perhaps the most comprehensive review that's ever been done. Although I understand PCE have done a similar one as well, which has come out with the same sort of patterns.

So that's what we're reporting back today, and then the next piece of work that we've still got to complete is the financial needs assessment that we're planning for at the moment. So once those three pieces of work are done, we can tick this off and say we've done a good job, and so far, so good. We're two-thirds of the way through. On the right, there's just a wee diagram of how the reference group interacts with assessment team, and there's a huge working group that Ian has as well of ecologists and other experts from around New Zealand that help him with

problem-solving. And next slide. Thank you. So thank you, Chris. Just to expand on the working group. So that's governmental, non-governmental, finance experts, biodiversity experts. There's about 26 of us on the working group, and we pull on the different skill sets as required as we go through the process.

It's quite important for us to say it's not a musical instrument, and it's not larger than life. Yep, and it's not a science. It's biodiversity finance. Keep one eye on the end game. As the economy grows, investment in biodiversity grows.

And so what I wanted to talk about here is simply where, if we had biodiversity investment tracking with economic growth, which is what we're suggesting as part of sustainable development, you'd have the light blue bars. What the fund will do will help us do more of that as move transition more towards sustainable development by investing in biodiversity as the economy grows.

And so it's an economic approach. The dark blue bars are current biodiversity spend, and so over the last 24 months, the cumulative reduction in biodiversity spend is $133 million, and that has biodiversity outcomes. Impacts on biodiversity income, impacts across New Zealand outcomes.

So yeah, when we get to the fund, if you were to draw some dotted lines or additional boxes above the dark blue bars, that's what we want to do, is fill some of that with this new fund, and that's where we seek full cross-party support.

Next slide Yes, so prevailing over biodiversity loss can't be solved the same way as before. New Zealand households actually spend more on cosmetics than biodiversity. Collapse of all critical global ecosystems is a high risk rating. Governments such as the UK government, Canadian government, IPBS, WB, UN, OECD, and WEF. Living Planet Index is -27 left from 50 years ago.

So it's declined and it's still declining. Mm. Urgent biodiversity investment is needed. New Zealand's biodiversity investment has declined to one point or 1,155 million in 2025/26. The cumulative natural capital deferral increases are 133 million in two years. Prolonged deferral is fiscal imprudence.

And just to, fiscal imprudence means ongoing financial mismanagement. And so for my background's economics from New Zealand, London School of Economics, and so we're saying reduce that fiscal imprudence and increase by increasing investment. So it's a nice easy equation.

So I wanted to talk a little bit about the results of the research Ian's done, and it really looked at all of the sectors of government and local government and other sectors like primary and business sectors, and how much is spent and where it's spent. So this is the core of it. So- Mm... this is a very complicated diagram of course.

It's, I think we call it the worm diagram, but the take homes are the size of the boxes on the left-hand side. And DOC of course- Goodness, I've got that on mine. DOC of course, is the by far the largest expenditure, but you can see that MPI and MFE are major contributors as well, and the rest of government and regional unitary councils, of course, major contributors as well. So, but also the voluntary sectors. You've got community trusts and NGOs that are making a massive amount of effort there, and they are often supported by councils as well.

So it tends to be a whole ecosystem of effort that goes into prioritizing at a very local level what's important to the people in the communities of those areas, and how do we deliver it together. And so that, the web side of it, to me, it's complicated and hard to understand, but it also gives it some resilience, I think, as well. So, business and finance in there with $5 million. So it's obviously of interest, of broad interest to everyone.

In the next slide, I put the right-hand side into an easier diagram that didn't have the worms on it, and that really shows where it's being spent. So understandably, mostly on conservation. But awareness of knowledge a lot on biosecurity, which is understandable given the impact that introduced pests have on our native ecosystems, but also sustainable use, planning and finance, a little bit on restoration and green economy.

And the P at the bottom is pollution management. That's only half a percent. But, these are all following, I think, your criteria, aren't they, that we have to follow using the biofin process. So some of the language used here isn't perhaps what New Zealand people would use. Did you have any comments on that, Ian? Yeah, so the key one out of all of these results was restoration at 4%, which is 0.01% of GDP.

And so, that's the area we've identified where we need to invest, and improve our investment as the economy grows. And so, 0.01% goes a long way, but if we were to double that to 0.02%, it would go a fantastic amount of distance in terms of maintaining and restoring what we call natural capital- Mm... in New Zealand. Yeah. So, restoration is the one of the, of all of the biofin

categories where it's been identified we need to do more. Are we just doing questions at the end? Sorry, just- Yeah. Just opening up for questions at the end. We'll let them talk through- Yeah... the presentation, and then we can have questions. I think slides were-- I think we've only got four slides to go, but yeah, this is, so this one's a summary of the recommendations that have come out of the second report that Ian's completed.

And firstly, can I just thank you for the cross-party support you've given last time we were here, and that is incredibly important I think, just because biodiversity does affect all of us, and it's for all of us and for our children. So that, I think, is our biggest ask is that can we continue that? Secondly, of course, complete the assessment, do that third report that we have to complete. We should have that done by Christmas, maybe a bit after, depending on how we go.

We've also been asked to draft a natural capital policy, and Ian's probably well placed to do that given his training. And then we'll talk soon about this business case as well for a natural capital fund, and I'll hand over to Ian on that. So thanks, Chris. Just the bottom note there, in terms of the fund, we're still maintaining our ask for all parties to commit to starting this fund at 25 million, as a minimum manifesto commitment, which equates to 2% of the current conservation budget. That would be targeted at the

most effective, efficient biodiversity outcomes that are currently unfunded in New Zealand. That equates to a $5 cup of coffee each year, or 0.006% of GDP. Might only be half a coffee now. Yeah, exactly. Depends on what coffee you buy. Yeah. So, and it's back to that graph where we have economy going up. What we're saying is that this helps fill a bit of the gap, so that

as the economy grows, we invest more in biodiversity. That's the principle. And that provides a step towards sustainable development. So, we'll just move on to recommendation one, which is a policy. That policy, and again, I'd just like to acknowledge Simon Court. He had the vision to say, "Yeah, I can see we need that," so I'd like to acknowledge him.

It simply says this is a natural capital asset that we're investing in, like a building, like a school, a hospital, a piece of machinery, an airplane fleet, a set of trains, road. It's an asset, so you maintain and restore it as you get benefits from it. So, the real key message there from the international community is, it's like a relationship. If your partner is just take, take, take, it's probably not going to work.

It's give and take, and that'll give you a good relationship, and that's the relationship we want with New Zealand biodiversity. So, yeah, natural capital policy says it's an asset and that we should reduce deferrals, as opposed to increase deferrals.

Recommendation two is the fund. We've sort of already talked about that. Our key message there is it's based on principles as opposed to anything else. So, it's indexed to growth, which provides the revenue stream. The revenue side of the instrument of the solution is the most efficient thing you will have in New Zealand, because it's indexed to consumption, because consumption is the largest indirect

driver of biodiversity loss. That's not disputed. Everyone from World Bank through to OECD through to the UN, it's an established fact. So, as we increase consumption, we invest more in biodiversity. So, it's indexed to GST growth, which is a proxy for consumption growth.

So, just one last thing there. It's a balancing loop. So, the system's balancing loop. So, if you're just consuming, without investing, it's never going to work. The other thing is it's independent. So, the best example of a fund that does this now is the super fund.

They have their guardians. It's invested in the future. It's a contribution. This is a fund which is invested in the future. It's a contribution as we consume. The third thing there, voluntary contributions. If the other organizations, which is going to be highly likely, want to make a contribution and say, "Well, we want to leave something behind,"

this fund is what they can contribute to. So, that's a bonus. Cost benefit targeting is an economic approach, and how it works is, and we do it in New Zealand already. For those who know the Next Foundation, they're fantastic at this. So, that's where the costs are low and the biodiversity benefits are high. That's where you invest.

So, it gives you the best cost-benefit ratio. And so, every project that gets approved must have that cost-benefit ratio to prove that it's doing what it says it will do, and then it's monitored. The last bit here is you're investing in ecological prospects for future generations.

The wording ecological prospects, I did get that from Next. And it's about making sure our children have the same opportunities we had for enjoying biodiversity. And it's just where, again, this fund, we're talking 0.006% of our GDP just to invest in future generations.

It's not even comparable to inflation, which happens every year at over a cent a year. So, initial results do show that that significantly outperforms things like credit schemes or plant a tree schemes. It would be fair to say I've just been invited to Kenya to talk to the UN about this new solution, because they can see the potential in it, and they want other countries to know about it.
So, I leave on Sunday to go and present it to them. Hopefully I don't come back with Ebola. The last recommendations we're suggesting, we finished the presentation. Thanks, Barbara.

We finished the assessment. She's left the room, but I really want to acknowledge Barbara Kuriger. She has been incredible from the start of this journey as our- You waited for her to leave. I know, I'm just saying it behind her back. She could tell it was about to happen. She has been a fantastic, incredible, amazing champion for this project across parties from the start. So I just wanted to give that- He spoke well of you too, Lam, before I came.

Yeah, he did speak highly of you. I have no doubt. He's a specialist at doing it when you're not here. PR 101, Ian. No, my apologies, though. I mentioned to Ian that I would be racing back from a speaking bit, and I am very sorry- It's all good... from the start.

It's so good to have you here, so thank you. So yeah, finished the assessment. So we've got two organizations who have participated in the first stage. We really need their participation in the second stage because the more they participate, the more they get out of it, and that's the Department of Conservation and Ministry of Primary Industries.

Primary Industries because of biosecurity. Department of Conservation because of their role in biodiversity. Now, in the last stage, they were hesitant to help because they felt because I talked to ministers, they felt like they shouldn't necessarily be talking to me. So I just need some support from Parliament to say, "Hey, it's all right to participate in the next stage." So be very grateful for that steer.

They are keen as mustard, but they're just wondering why there isn't support. So yeah, just wanted to mention that that would really help because the more we work together, the more robust our investment case will be. Then the last recommendation, and I'm very grateful for two pretty amazing people from the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment, is that we do this again, and so in 2029. So this is a strategic long-term thing.

It's not a short-term thing. And so we do it again, do the assessment again, and that the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Environment would, in terms of their purpose, they have the right purpose to lead this with support from other organizations.

A lot of the support I got in terms of understanding how I needed to reach out to government departments, I was very grateful for the advice I was given from the PCE. That's our recommendations. I believe that's our presentation, and I'd like to thank you very much for your time, and we'd love to answer any questions you have.

Oh, thank you very much, Ian, for that presentation. Look, we have got a few questions. We will start with Lam. Kia ora. Thank you so much. First, just the initial question on your, I don't know, as one of the- Worm... squares. No, not the worm, the squares. It was just basic. You don't need to go back to it, actually.

Yep, I know the one. Yeah But just the green economy part, it was only 3%. I would think that would be a bigger- Yeah, so-... part. So what's the definition there, and what are you- Yeah. So Biophina is a United Nations methodology that's used in 133 countries. We use what's called an attribution process. So the focus is on biodiversity, including biosecurity. So if I'm spending $100 million on solar panels, we would count, say, 3%, 4%, 5% of that towards biodiversity.

Mm-hmm. Compared to, say, a next model where they're doing work on directly with biodiversity or Department of Conservation's conservation budget. We would go 80%, 90%, 100% of the attribution of that $100 million would be counted. Okay. So that's the reason, is how we attribute the investment- Okay... specifically for biodiversity.

Thank you. And Priyanka, yes. My question related to that was then, given that the green economy spend is 3%, restoration is 4%, you mentioned that restoration is really where we should be investing in. And I wanted to know why. Is that because a cost-benefit analysis there, that every dollar that you spend in restoration yields more directly to biodiversity protection, or was there a different reason for that?

Yeah, that's a great question. And initial testing, yes, you're going to get a much higher cost-benefit ratio from that investment. It's also an area where we're not improving the asset, and New Zealand's in that position now where we need to be improving that asset. And so it's also purpose-driven. It's not to say, for example, green economy doesn't need more investment, because it certainly does.

But for biodiversity outcomes, that's where you're going to get bang for buck, or money. Grant, you've got a supplement It's got support on that also into this restoration bit. So I'm just curious how you got your figures about restoration from, because does it include what private people are doing? How would you know?

Some of the work that, for example, is done on farms. Mm. How was that? I'm just curious. All right. Yeah. Good question. So I'm going to use a phrase here, which I still snuck into the report without anyone telling me off too much. So the primary industry spend, which is about 55 million, comes from Beef and Lamb have really good figures.

They do an annual environmental expenditure, so Beef and Lamb provided that, or Sheep and Beef as they like me to call it. And so fisheries, that came from, is it Seafood New Zealand? Mm. Dairy came from Dairy New Zealand. So those numbers came from them.

The private sector, in terms of the NGOs, getting those figures was worse than drinking a warm cup of cat sick. It really was. That's the first time I've read that in a report. So there's 1,200 NGOs registered on the Charity Services register. Anything over a million dollars, we went through their annual report. So that took quite a while.

Ian, can I just mention too, so from Beef and Lamb's point of view, I'm a monitored farm. Yep. So what happens there is that every year I sit down with someone from Beef and Lamb. They go through line by line my financials, and we identify what was spent on biodiversity, all that side of things.

So it is quite a thorough- Example of fencing, pest control- Yep... planting- Yes... that type of thing. Anything else on this? Yep. Celia. Thank you very much. That's great for farming landowners. Is there anything collected about what people who've got basically carbon farms or are small land holders that aren't members of those large groups?

You mean life season spark holders are what you're talking about? Hmm? Life season spark holders. Oh, season. Oh, my. Oh, God. So unless we captured it under the non-governmental organizations as investment, we weren't able to capture those. You wouldn't have that. That's fine. I couldn't see how you could.

Yeah. Yeah. But that's interesting. Okay. So what we also captured though, as part of the NGOs, is an estimate of $49 million worth of voluntary hours. That's an underestimate. Yeah. So New Zealanders are saying, "We want this work done anyway." And did- Yeah. Yep... and did that include Predator Free New Zealand Trust?

Correct. Yes. Okay. Yeah, Predator Free Trust. The whole lot. And all, yeah, all the work that Nex does with them. Yeah. So Jesse Morgan and the rest as well. Catchment groups. Sorry? You do catchment groups? Okay. Yes. So Chris can talk to the council numbers if you want.

Yeah. Just- Yes. It's supported by either NPI on Farm or regional councils or both. Mm. Catchment groups are very well covered, I think. Okay. Mm. And I was thinking to your question, a lot of people will be seeking funding from councils, whether regional or otherwise, and also from trusts. Like in our region we have Bay Trust and also some energy trusts who've increasingly got into the space- Mm... of environmental contributions.

So quite often you'll find people who are doing work in the environment will be seeking co-funding or contributions. Mm. And in fact, that became a bit of a problem for Ian, because then we had to go through and make sure we weren't double counting it. Yeah. Yeah. Because it was counted once by regional council, once by Bay Trust, and then- Mm... the landowner might have put the same number in there.

So that was quite a rigorous process, as I recall, going through- Mm. Well, actually-... quite a handful of them... useful. Yeah. I did wonder though why you only put regional and unitary, because I know at least in Eden and Wellington city councils put in a fairly walloping amount of rate payers' money.

So the- Did that get included, just the title or? So the answer to that is lack of resources. So had to focus on what I could add up. Okay. No. So I couldn't include the territorials or the locals. Where we have been able to capture some of their numbers is if they've made contributions to an NGO, then we capture it there. So NGOs spend 100 million a year plus the 49 million- Mm... on voluntary hours, but their actual spend is something like 238 million because they also get additional funding from regional councils and central government

that they deliver. They are actually the second biggest delivery body in New Zealand. Mm. Thank you. I'll come back with more questions. Yeah, we've just got a couple of other questions around the table. So Priyanka. Thanks. I had a question when I read your report, Ian, on work like what Botham School's doing around credits, nature credits- Yep... financing. I see in your PowerPoint presentation as well that you've said that your fund is more effective than credits.

Yep. So wanting to understand that a little bit better, and also work out how existing work in that space fits into this. Yep. Mm. So credits have, so by VCD projects, the one way to look at it, just one way, is those projects are there already. Mm. And so if you've got $100, you want $100 going into that project. And so the administration on the fund is Is kept very low so that the $100 go in.

With credit schemes, they are usually attached to conditions, usually commercial conditions. They also have an admin cost that goes over the top of it, same with offsets. And also, there's also the where are we finding the money from. And so that's a massive cost internationally as well.

And so just to also put credits into the global scheme. So biodiversity finance across the glo- globally is over 100 billion. You've got United Nations environment programme measure it every year. Of that portion, 18% is private, 82% is public. So most of the innovation is actually happening in the public sector. The reason for that is because biodiversity has public good characteristics- Mm... like policing, some parts of the health system, governance. So it's public. And so of that, there's

5% in offsets and credits, and of that, I think 1% is credits internationally. Mm-hmm. But there's definitely opportunity to grow the market. Yeah. Right? But you're always going to have a lot of cost on that. And talking to the biodiversity credit firms that are doing it in New Zealand- Mm-hmm... they're saying it's a lot of administration at the moment.

So is there a way to include that in your fund sort of model, or is this a parallel model? Yes. So in terms, yes and no. So the yes is it'll be included in the BioFin assessment. It won't be included in the fund because it's a separate thing.

Okay. So the overall funding from New Zealand will be a mix of funding tools. Mm-hmm. The fund will just be, like I said, it's just 2% of the total. Mm-hmm. Yeah. But it'll be highly targeted in principle to do cost benefit targeting. Yeah.

Thank you. Look, we have got a question from Sam Fundel. Oh, yeah. I have all these wonderful bay boys here. It's good. Hey, you mentioned there about the 82%. I'm assuming you meant that that's spending from the, is that of the spending pool? That's from the public sector. Correct. Yeah, so. Yeah, correct.

And generally that's from green bonds, right? Where they'll borrow from investors, the government will borrow from investors, pay them a coupon, and then use that money to finance different environmental projects. So the answer to the question is that's a small part of it.

Oh, okay. Yeah. So there's at the moment, there's 150 different methods that the international community raises finance, where in New Zealand we've got, say, five or six key ones like rates and doing credits and votes, stuff like that. Okay.

NGO. So they do bonds, they do off all sorts of stuff. A lot of the government funding internationally is similar to our votes. So it's a government allocation for a purpose. As you no doubt know, one of the things we'll look at in New Zealand is green bonds, and using that green bonds revenue or portion of it for biodiversity.

Mm-hmm. I think that's a good idea. Mm-hmm. We- And, Cameron. Oh, straight into me. Thank you. Yeah. Thank you. And then I'll go to Lan. Lovely. Okay. Well, my question, thank you. While speaking, I've just got a question about, this committee's just been through a large process on the new planning and natural environment bills. And in there, there's the regulatory relief function.

Do you think that your BioFin methodology will be a way for councils to accurately-ish measure the regulatory burdens they're putting on when they go to make a planning measure or regulation on a private landowner? And a way we can value other things, like whether this is justified, whether there's another way to do it.

Do you see this methodology being utilized in that regard? So I think they're complementary things rather than the fund will do that. So the fund is- Well, that's about the methodology more, but- Yeah... sure. Yeah. Yeah. Sorry, rather the fund, but yeah. So, the purpose of the fund is to improve the asset.

So that's the purpose of the fund. So what you're possibly talking about is research and policy, that'll be our, our focus will be on restoration- I guess I'm asking, like the fund is going to have to know what it's doing, right? You're going to have to have- Yeah... methodologies to figure out biodiversity values, whether this is the best path to go.

Yeah. Like the method. And so, is this going to be something that's open to councils to be able to use? Do you think it becomes a recognizable process? Yes. So yes, the answer to that question, yes. Yeah. Excellent. Mm-hmm. Which was kind of my question actually, was around how the RMA and changing the resource management system, how BioFin sits alongside that or how you kind of see that.

Do you want to talk to that a bit? Yeah, it's a really interesting question, and I think some of us are still wrapping our heads around- Mm... the significance of the decisions that have been just released. And I think we're talking about apples and oranges though. Mm-hmm. So one thing is a regulatory, how do we regulate for biodiversity, and I think that's a very complex problem for New Zealand, and the RMA tried one way, and now we're going to try it a different way. But this is non-regulatory.

This is investing in the environment. No, I think that's part of the- So this is more like the predator free thing. But that's part of the options in the new system is saying- You don't necessarily have to regulate. You can try these other ways, more consents, more development opportunities, or at least have investment come in. So do you-- Yeah. Obviously something you'd like to say, you're trying to get your head around it- Yeah... and trying to work with it.

It could work. Mm. But so it is complementary- It's, it's-... in that sense, yes. Complementary. Excellent. Um, Lam, your question. Yeah, no. Unworkable. But- Oh, in your opinion. Interested in, coming back to the fund, I know governments have different priorities, and they're always going to be stretched for money.

What is sort of your selling point in terms of... Because, for example, the Community Environment Fund was scrapped by this government. What is the selling point of this fund and, because it's pri-- If I understand it correctly, it's like prioritizing the low-hanging fruit or like the biggest bang for buck kind of projects versus a general slash community fund that will actually fund grassroots restoration and biodiversity.

How would you describe the difference? So the purpose of this fund is to invest in biodiversity so that your core... And keeping in mind, it's 0.006% of GDP, so we're not talking a huge allocation of our economy. It doesn't prohibit, nor should it prohibit, having community funds where you're getting wider benefits. I think that's fantastic.

This fund will be very targeted, similar to the next model in some ways. Can I just jump in there from a practical point of view? Sorry, I don't . Yeah, that's good. So, on the ground, a fund like this is really good in the fact that, A, there's not going to be a whole lot of bureaucracy in the middle.

One of the biggest things about biodiversity is that so often, people who are working on the ground get tied up in admin, in a whole lot of other things, and it doesn't put trees in the ground. Mm. It doesn't do trapping. It doesn't do all those sort of things.

A fund like this is going to sit out the independent, just like QE2, which is complementary to this. Mm-hmm. And it'll mean you're going to get a lot more bang for your buck. That's the really- And ongoing continuity- On, yes, exactly... on the ground, right? Yeah. It's not going to fall off a cliff each time a government changes, that sort of thing.
